title: From Ballia to Beijing: How an IAS Officer Turned UP's Forgotten Sattu Into a Global Superfood Brand
excerpt: Rebranded as 'Sattu Pops' under the One District One Product scheme, Ballia's traditional roasted gram flour is now sold on Amazon, stocked in post offices, and served in Chinese university cafeterias.
body:
• Ballia's traditional sattu — roasted gram flour once considered a low-prestige food of labourers — has been rebranded as 'Sattu Pops' and is now being served in Chinese university cafeterias.
  • IAS officer Aojasvi Raj revived the district's fading sattu economy by organizing more than 700 women from self-help groups into a production and packaging network.
  • Gram cultivation in Ballia has more than doubled in two years, and sattu entrepreneurs in the district are building businesses worth crores.
  • The product earned One District One Product recognition, is available on Amazon and Blinkit, and is sold through 100 post offices across Uttar Pradesh.

The Superfood Nobody Took Seriously

Sattu has been part of India's food culture for millennia. During the Vedic period, barley seeds were pulverized into a powder called saktu — the precursor to modern sattu. For centuries, it was the fuel of labourers and farmers across the Gangetic plain: mixed with water, salt, and green chillies for an instant, no-cook meal that could be carried in a cloth bundle and eaten anywhere.

But that working-class association became sattu's biggest liability. As Krishnendu Ray, associate professor of food studies at New York University, has noted, sattu "carried low prestige and ranked lower in the urban hierarchy of taste among city dwellers, from middle-class Bengalis of Kolkata to Delhiite professionals." While quinoa and chia seeds from South America became global superfoods, sattu — with 20 grams of protein and 7 grams of fibre per 100-gram serving — stayed invisible.

An IAS Officer Sees What Everyone Missed

When IAS officer Aojasvi Raj took charge as Chief Development Officer in Ballia, a district in eastern Uttar Pradesh historically famous for its gram and sattu production, the picture was bleak. Poor returns had pushed farmers away from growing gram. Young people were leaving. Ballia was losing its identity.

Raj saw the gap between what the world was paying for imported protein powders and what Ballia already had. His approach was not to build a factory but to mobilize the people who already knew how to make sattu. More than 700 women from self-help groups were organized into a production chain — roasting the gram, removing husks, grinding it into flour, and packaging the finished product.

"Ballia didn't need a new industry. It simply needed someone to believe in its oldest one."

— The Better India, on IAS officer Aojasvi Raj's sattu revival

From Brown Packets to Premium Branding

The transformation went beyond production. Simple brown packets were replaced with premium gift boxes featuring nutritional information, new flavours, recipe booklets, and Ballia's cultural story. Sattu was repositioned not as a poor man's ration but as a modern vegan protein — the Indian answer to whey powder.

The rebrand worked. Ballia's sattu earned One District One Product (ODOP) recognition from the Uttar Pradesh government, opening doors to institutional support, marketing, and exports. The products are now available on Amazon and Blinkit. In August 2025, the district launched sales through 100 post offices across the Varanasi postal region, with plans to expand nationwide.

Gram cultivation in Ballia has more than doubled in two years. Sattu entrepreneurs in the district are generating revenues in crores. The administration is planning protein bars, protein powder variants, and larger processing units to meet growing demand.

Chinese University Cafes and the Global Push

The most unexpected milestone came when Ballia's rebranded sattu products — marketed as "Sattu Pops" — appeared on the menu at Chinese university cafeterias. The crossover from eastern UP to Chinese campuses illustrates both the product's nutritional appeal and the ODOP scheme's ambition to take hyperlocal Indian products global.

Sattu's nutritional profile makes the case easily. At roughly 20 grams of protein per 100-gram serving, it competes with commercial protein powders at a fraction of the price. Unlike most protein supplements, sattu is naturally cooling — a property Ayurvedic tradition attributes to the dry-roasting process — making it particularly suited to hot climates. It requires no cooking, mixes instantly with water, and has an indefinite shelf life when stored dry.

Part of a Larger Revival

Ballia's success is part of a broader moment for traditional Indian ingredients. If 2025 was the year of millets — driven by the International Year of Millets campaign — 2026 is shaping up as sattu's year. Metropolitan cafes now serve sattu lattes, Instagram is full of sattu smoothie bowls, and ITC recently launched Aashirvaad Chana Sattu in Bihar and West Bengal.

The Uttar Pradesh government has announced ODOP 2.0, which will focus on scaling successful first-phase enterprises, along with a One District One Cuisine programme to brand each district's signature food. For the diaspora, Ballia's story is a reminder that India's next global food export may not come from a lab or a startup — it may come from a self-help group in a district most people have never heard of.
image_caption: Sattu, a roasted gram flour from eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, is gaining recognition as a high-protein superfood. An IAS officer's initiative has helped take the traditional staple from Ballia to international markets.
nri_angle: NRIs seeking affordable Indian protein alternatives to Western supplements can now order Ballia's sattu products on Amazon; the ODOP success story shows Indian food heritage going global.
